ai.definition: Blockchain for decentralized identity management is a technology that leverages blockchain's immutable ledger to create secure, self-sovereign digital identities. These identities are stored on a distributed network without relying on central authorities.
ai.howItWorks: Each identity transaction or update is recorded as a block in the blockchain, creating an unalterable and transparent history of the identity’s lifecycle. Users control their own keys to authenticate transactions, ensuring that only they can manage their data.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing issues such as identity theft, fraud, and privacy breaches by providing a tamper-proof and decentralized solution for managing digital identities.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves developing smart contracts and cryptographic protocols to ensure the security and integrity of the blockchain network. No physical goods are manufactured; rather, it is software development focused.
ai.buildProcess: Developers create and test smart contracts that define the rules for identity verification and data access. These contracts are then deployed on a blockchain platform such as Ethereum or Hyperledger Fabric.
ai.costDrivers: Costs primarily stem from the computational resources required to maintain the blockchain network, including hardware infrastructure and energy consumption. Development costs include software development, testing, and security audits.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to grow as more industries recognize its potential for enhancing privacy and reducing fraud in digital identity management.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are still evolving. Current challenges include ensuring compliance with data protection laws like GDPR while maintaining the decentralized nature of blockchain systems.
ai.risks: Technical risks include vulnerabilities in smart contracts, scalability issues, and the potential for 51% attacks on smaller networks. Non-technical risks involve legal and regulatory uncertainties.
ai.profitability: Profitability is largely dependent on adoption by businesses and governments. While there are costs associated with implementation, long-term benefits such as reduced fraud and improved privacy can lead to cost savings.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving scalability, interoperability between different blockchain networks, and enhancing user experience through more intuitive interfaces.

glossary.def: A method of managing digital identities without relying on central authorities.
Automated, self-executing contracts with the terms directly written into code.
An identity that is controlled by the individual rather than a third party.
A type of attack where an entity gains control over more than 50% of the network’s computing power to manipulate the blockchain.

subsystems.name: Identity registry (ledger)
subsystems.role: anchors DIDs and revocation data on a tamper-evident, decentralized network.

subsystems.name: DID resolver
subsystems.role: maps a DID to its DID document, which contains public keys and service endpoints.

subsystems.name: Wallet
subsystems.role: lets a person hold their private keys and verifiable credentials securely.

subsystems.name: Issuer platform
subsystems.role: allows organisations to issue verifiable credentials to holders.

subsystems.name: Verifier platform
subsystems.role: checks that presented credentials are authentic, unrevoked and from a trusted issuer.

subsystems.name: Governance framework
subsystems.role: defines who may issue which credentials and how trust is established.

buildSteps.title: Choose or define a DID method
buildSteps.detail: Specify exactly how identifiers are created, written to a ledger, resolved and deactivated — for example a method built on Ethereum or Hyperledger Indy.

buildSteps.title: Deploy the ledger components
buildSteps.detail: Set up nodes and smart contracts or transaction types that record DIDs and revocation lists without exposing personal data.

buildSteps.title: Implement the resolver
buildSteps.detail: Write software that reads the ledger and returns the correct DID document for any supported DID method.

buildSteps.title: Build the wallet
buildSteps.detail: Create an app that generates and stores private keys in secure hardware, and holds verifiable credentials the user receives.

buildSteps.title: Create issuer tools
buildSteps.detail: Build services that let an organisation define credential schemas, sign credentials with its keys and publish revocation information.

buildSteps.title: Create verifier tools
buildSteps.detail: Build libraries that request credentials, verify signatures against the issuer’s DID, check revocation status and apply trust rules.

buildSteps.title: Establish revocation and status
buildSteps.detail: Implement a privacy-preserving way to revoke or suspend credentials, such as status lists or cryptographic accumulators.

buildSteps.title: Agree governance
buildSteps.detail: Write the legal and technical rules: who can issue which claims, which schemas are valid, and how disputes are handled.

buildSteps.title: Pilot and iterate
buildSteps.detail: Run limited deployments with real users, measure usability and security, then widen participation.

prerequisites.why: credentials and DID documents rely on keys to prove control and authenticity.
provides the decentralized, tamper-evident registry for DIDs and revocation data.

prerequisites.tech: W3C Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) and Verifiable Credentials standards
prerequisites.why: the core specifications exist but tooling, profiles and interoperability are still maturing.
wallets need tamper-resistant storage for private keys to prevent theft.
lets users prove a claim without revealing extra personal data, but performance and standardisation are still improving.

pathway.milestone: government and enterprise pilots, such as the European Union’s eIDAS 2.0 digital identity wallet effort
pathway.unlocks: real-world testing of wallets, issuers and verifiers with citizens and customers.
credentials that work no matter which blockchain or app a person uses.

pathway.milestone: integration with existing web identity protocols like OpenID Connect
pathway.unlocks: easier adoption by services that already support conventional login.
reduced reliance on centralised identity providers and fewer large-scale identity theft risks.
